title: CAP, Consistency & ACID vs BASE
summary: Every distributed system makes a silent trade-off: consistency or availability when the network fails. Master CAP, PACELC, and ACID vs BASE to reason clearly about any distributed database.

blocks.markdown:
In a distributed system, **nodes fail and networks split**. The CAP theorem says you can't keep all three: Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance.

- Every distributed database picks a side: **CP** (correct answers, may reject requests) or **AP** (always responds, may return stale data).
- ACID and BASE are the transaction philosophies that follow from that choice.
- Understanding this trade-off is the foundation for reasoning about [nosql-modern-databases](nosql-modern-databases) and [distributed-databases](distributed-databases).

**CAP theorem** (Brewer, 2000): a distributed data store can guarantee at most **two** of three properties simultaneously.

- **Consistency (C)** — every read returns the most recent write, or an error.
- **Availability (A)** — every request gets a non-error response (may not be the latest data).
- **Partition tolerance (P)** — the system continues operating even when network messages between nodes are lost or delayed.

A **network partition** is when two groups of nodes can't communicate, e.g. a datacenter link goes down.

- **CA** (consistent + available, no partition tolerance) only exists in a single-node system — any real network can partition.
- In practice the choice is always **CP vs AP**.

blocks.subTitle: Why P is non-negotiable
blocks.markdown:
**Partition tolerance is not optional** in any real distributed system.

- Networks drop packets, cables fail, datacenters go dark. You cannot prevent partitions — only respond to them.
- If you drop P, you have a single-machine system and CAP no longer applies.
- So the real design question is: **when a partition happens, do you keep C or A?**

CP: refuse reads/writes until the partition heals. AP: serve possibly-stale data and reconcile later.

blocks.subTitle: CP vs AP examples
blocks.markdown:
Real systems pick a side.

| System | Choice | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|
| HBase / Zookeeper | CP | Financial/config data — stale is wrong |
| Cassandra / DynamoDB | AP | Always available; reconcile conflicts later |
| Spanner | CP (near-CA) | TrueTime gives tight consistency |

Note: most databases let you tune per-operation (e.g. Cassandra's quorum levels), so the choice isn't always binary.

**PACELC** extends CAP to cover normal (non-partition) operation.

- **If Partition** (P): choose **A** vs **C** — same as CAP.
- **Else** (E — normal operation): choose **L**atency vs **C**onsistency.

Even without failures, making a write consistent across replicas adds **latency** (you wait for acknowledgements). PACELC forces you to name that cost explicitly.

Example: DynamoDB is PA/EL — available during partitions, low-latency (eventual) in normal ops. Spanner is PC/EC — consistent in both cases, higher latency.

"Consistency" in CAP is coarse. In practice there's a spectrum.

- **Strong consistency** — after a write completes, every subsequent read from any node returns that value. Feels like a single machine.
- **Causal consistency** — writes that are causally related are seen in order by all nodes. Unrelated writes may appear out of order.
- **Eventual consistency** — if no new writes occur, all replicas will converge to the same value — but they may diverge temporarily.

blocks.subTitle: Strong vs eventual in practice
blocks.markdown:
Choosing a consistency level is a latency–correctness trade-off.

- **Strong**: need coordinator acknowledgement before returning — adds round-trips. Use for balances, inventory, anything where stale = wrong.
- **Causal**: good for social feeds (your own posts visible to you before others). Libraries like vector clocks track causality.
- **Eventual**: DNS, shopping carts, "likes" counters — briefly stale is acceptable, and you get the lowest latency.

See [sharding-replication-scaling](sharding-replication-scaling) for how replication lag creates these windows.

A **quorum** is the minimum number of nodes that must agree for an operation to succeed.

- **N** = total replicas. **W** = nodes that must confirm a write. **R** = nodes that must respond to a read.
- **Rule: R + W > N** guarantees that every read overlaps with the latest write — you always see the freshest copy.
- Example: N=3, W=2, R=2 → R+W=4 > 3. At least one node in every read set has the latest write.

Quorum is the mechanism AP systems use to dial consistency level per-operation.

blocks.subTitle: Quorum trade-offs
blocks.markdown:
Tuning N, W, R lets you slide between consistency and throughput.

- **W=1, R=N** — fast writes, slow reads (read-heavy apps).
- **W=N, R=1** — slow writes, fast reads.
- **W=1, R=1** — maximum throughput, no consistency guarantee.
- **R+W > N** — the only configuration that guarantees you'll always read the latest write.

Cassandra exposes this as `ONE`, `QUORUM`, `ALL` consistency levels per query.

**ACID** is the transaction model of classic relational databases — strong guarantees, single-machine roots.

- **Atomicity** — a transaction is all-or-nothing; partial writes never persist.
- **Consistency** — a transaction moves the DB from one valid state to another (all constraints satisfied).
- **Isolation** — concurrent transactions behave as if they ran sequentially.
- **Durability** — once committed, data survives crashes (written to disk/WAL).

See [transactions-acid](transactions-acid) for deep isolation levels.

**BASE** is the alternative model embraced by AP NoSQL systems, optimizing for availability and scale.

- **Basically Available** — the system responds to every request, though data may be stale or partially written.
- **Soft state** — state may change over time even without a write, as replicas converge asynchronously.
- **Eventual consistency** — given no new writes, all replicas will converge to the same value eventually.

BASE trades correctness guarantees for availability and lower latency.

blocks.subTitle: ACID vs BASE
blocks.markdown:
Choosing between them is choosing a system's failure mode.

| Property | ACID | BASE |
|---|---|---|
| Consistency | Strong, immediate | Eventual |
| Availability | May reject during failure | Always responds |
| Best for | Payments, inventory | Social feeds, caches |

ACID says "refuse if I can't be correct." BASE says "respond now, fix later."

Common mistakes when reasoning about CAP and consistency:

- **"CA databases exist."** A CA system is just a single-node system. Any real network can partition.
- **"Eventual consistency = no consistency."** It's a defined guarantee — convergence is real, just not instant.
- **"ACID and BASE are mutually exclusive."** Distributed databases like CockroachDB and Spanner achieve ACID over multiple nodes using consensus protocols (Raft, Paxos).
- **"Tuning W=1 is safe."** Without R+W>N, your reads may miss the latest write under concurrent load.

blocks.subTitle: The CAP theorem
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Explain the CAP theorem.**

A distributed store can guarantee at most two of: Consistency (every read gets the latest write), Availability (every request gets a response), Partition tolerance (works through network failures). Since partitions are inevitable, the real choice is **CP** (correct, may refuse) vs **AP** (always responds, may be stale). Examples: Zookeeper is CP, Cassandra is AP.

blocks.subTitle: Can a system be CA?
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Can a database be both consistent and available — CA?**

Only in a single-node system where there are no partitions to handle. The moment you add a second node, a network partition becomes possible, and you must choose C or A when it occurs. Claiming CA in a distributed system just means you haven't thought about partition handling.

blocks.subTitle: ACID vs BASE
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is the difference between ACID and BASE?**

ACID (relational DBs) prioritizes correctness: transactions are atomic, isolated, and durable — the DB refuses rather than return wrong data. BASE (NoSQL AP systems) prioritizes availability: always respond, allow soft state, converge eventually. Pick ACID for financial or inventory data; BASE for feeds, counters, or caches where brief staleness is acceptable.

blocks.subTitle: Eventual consistency
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is eventual consistency? Is it safe?**

Eventual consistency guarantees that, given no new writes, all replicas will converge to the same value — but they may briefly disagree. It is safe for many workloads (DNS, social timelines, like counts) where seeing a slightly stale value for milliseconds causes no harm. It is unsafe for bank balances or inventory where a stale read leads to incorrect decisions.

blocks.subTitle: Quorum rule
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What does R + W > N guarantee in a distributed system?**

With N replicas, if any write is acknowledged by W nodes and any read queries R nodes, then R+W > N ensures those two sets always overlap — at least one node in the read set has the latest write. This makes a quorum read equivalent to a strongly consistent read, even in an eventually consistent system, at the cost of higher latency.

blocks.subTitle: PACELC
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What does PACELC add over CAP?**

CAP only describes the partition case. PACELC adds the **else** case: when the system is running normally (no partition), you still face a trade-off between **latency** and **consistency**. Making a write consistent across replicas requires waiting for acknowledgements, adding latency. PACELC makes this cost explicit and lets you classify systems on both axes.
